transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~30 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Evan Martinez (NimbleHead), Sara Liu (Nimble PM), Marcus Reed (Nimble SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): Review of last week's throughput runs; concurrency target tuning; queue-based smoothing; artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet link, config YAML, doc: redwood batching guide.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check, Evan can you hear me all good?
[00:04] Evan: Yep loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:07] Alex: Cool, we'll keep this to 30, Priya and I will run through the numbers, the spreadsheet we posted in the chat, and then tune the batching and queueing params.
[00:15] Priya: hi all, i'll share my screen in a sec, the run we did yesterday was the 1h ramp to 48 conc and steady 30 min at target before ramp down, i put the logs in the bench sheet link (https://app.redwood/bench/nimble) - note sometimes the link gets truncated in the transcript
[00:32] Sara: got it, thanks. quick reminder our SLO is p99 latency < 250ms for interactive paths, background bulk ops are ok to be higher.
[00:40] Marcus: and we care about cost; last month's estimates from our cloud team put hosted tokens at X, so any batching/caching wins matter.
[00:49] Priya: yep. so high level results: throughput (tokens/sec) improved ~22% when enabling continuous batching with max_batch_size 64 and batch_timeout 12ms versus baseline. however we saw p99 spikes during concurrency peaks, particularly when concurrency > 40.
[01:05] Evan: that matches what we saw internally, tail latencies jump, sometimes bursts of 800ms - 1.2s at the worst sample.
[01:12] Alex: ok that's crucial. Priya, can you walk through why the p99 spiked even though token throughput increased?
[01:16] Priya: sure, two reasons: one is head-of-line blocking in the local request queue when a large request (long context) lands and ties up a slot; second is KV cache misses causing backend recompute overhead. our continuous batching pools requests by model/seq_len but variable seq lengths can still cause stragglers.
[01:36] Marcus: is that the K V cash you mentioned last time? (small laugh)
[01:40] Priya: yeah that's the transcription of KV cache, haha. the other artifact is our current orchestration allows concurrency spikes to saturate a single instance; we can set concurrency per-instance caps and a shaping queue to smooth inbound load.
[01:52] Sara: what are the practical knobs? we don't want to throttle too low and blow up cost.
[01:56] Priya: practical knobs: 1) max_concurrency_per_worker (sets per-GPU parallel inferences), 2) request_queue_depth and queue_shed_policy (how many inflight queued), 3) batch_timeout_ms and max_batch_size, 4) prefix/KV cache pinning for warm traffic. plus warmup to keep KV hot.
[02:17] Alex: and Redwood has policy routing if we want to spill to a cheaper model variant during sustained bursts?
[02:21] Priya: yes, we can route to a quantized variant or smaller model for lower-cost tail mitigation; fallback policies are in the config we shared.
[02:27] Evan: is that automatic or we have to configure?
[02:30] Priya: you configure thresholds: e.g., if queue latency > 80ms and CPU/GPU util > 85% we can route certain requests to a fallback model. it's not magic, needs thresholds.
[02:40] Marcus: curious on the steady-state target; earlier we targeted 48 concurrency across cluster. is that per-instance or aggregate?
[02:45] Priya: that's aggregate. per instance we set target_concurrency to 6-8 depending on the GPU profile. in the last run we accidentally pushed 12 on one worker due to autoscaler bucketing which caused the p99 spikes.
[02:57] Alex: ok that explains the saturation. Evan, could you confirm your autoscaler config? are you using burst instances?
[03:03] Evan: we're using the standard cluster autoscaler rules; there was one config mismatch where pod anti-affinity allowed bin-packing. we'll tweak.
[03:10] Priya: recommendation: set max_concurrency_per_worker to 8, max_batch_size 48, batch_timeout_ms to 10-15ms, and enable request_queue with depth 200 and FCFS or priority buckets for interactive vs background. that smooths spikes and keeps p99 smaller.
[03:28] Sara: if we set queue depth that high, won't requests sit longer like increased avg latency?
[03:31] Priya: average might go up by 10-30ms but p99 drops sharply. we're trading a slight avg increase for tail stability. also queueing short-circuits long context items to different priority buckets.
[03:43] Evan: can we limit context len per fast path? we have some flows that send 6k tokens occasionally.
[03:48] Priya: yes, set a max_seq_len for the low-latency route and route longer contexts to a background worker pool; that's in the routing config. we also recommend using prefix/KV cache to keep repeated histories hot saw ~15% token reduction for chat flows in the bench.
[04:05] Marcus: any quick wins on quantization? we tried 4-bit and saw lower per-token cost but quality slip on some examples.
[04:12] Alex: this ties into the model profiling we did; Priya?
[04:14] Priya: quantization helped throughput but increased variance on some prompts; for the POC we suggest keeping hosted mainline model for interactive path and optionally enable quantized variant for bulk/rerank. our routing can pick per-route model variants.
[04:27] Sara: good. can you explain the steady-state 2-hour run you suggested? what will it show beyond the 1h sample?
[04:33] Priya: the longer run exposes memory pressure and KV cache churn under realistic diurnal or batched traffic; short runs can miss subtle memory growth or background GC. also it shows autoscaler behavior over sustained load.
[04:42] Evan: ok we can schedule 2-hour run at concurrency=48, but we want to try both config A (no queue, higher per-worker concurrency) and config B (queue + per-worker cap) to compare.
[04:53] Priya: perfect, that's what we recommend: A vs B comparison with identical synthetic traffic CSV. we'll annotate the bench sheet with which run is which.
[04:59] Alex: i'll share a template for the traffic CSV and the bench sheet after the call.
[05:03] Marcus: small nit, we saw one error in the logs around KMS: azure kms handshake error during the 3rd minute; prob unrelated but flagged.
[05:11] Priya: good catch please paste the log lines, we can cross-check with our KMS integration team; sometimes transient network issues with key rotation cause brief failures that cascade into retries and queuing anomalies.
[05:23] Evan: will do.
[05:25] Sara: also security ask: can we get SOC2 docs and network diagram for the private deployment?
[05:31] Alex: yes, we'll share SOC 2 summary and a private-deploy top-level network diagram. expect that in the security packet.
[05:38] Priya: on the ops side, I'll include the YAML snips: concurrency_per_worker, queue_depth, batch_timeout_ms, queue_shed_policy, fallback_model_id. that should make it plug-and-play for your infra team.
[05:49] Evan: timeline?
[05:50] Priya: we'll get the YAML and bench spreadsheet by end of day Friday (2026-10-09), Alex will add cost projection by 2026-10-08, and then you run the 2-hour tests next week and drop results in the sheet.
[06:03] Alex: quick recap then: 1) Redwood to share bench sheet & configs 2) Nimble to run A vs B 2-hour steady-state tests and paste logs 3) check KMS error lines and follow up 4) schedule on-prem benchmark week of 10/18 if results look good.
[06:17] Evan: sounds good.
[06:20] Sara: thanks team. one last question: any recommended concurrency target for a T4-like instance?
[06:25] Priya: for T4-like you should aim 6-8 effective concurrency for interactive, higher for bulk; with continuous batching you can increase throughput but watch p99.
[06:34] Marcus: ok thanks.
[06:36] Alex: great, we'll send notes and action items. Thanks everyone, we'll sync next week same time.
[06:41] Evan: thanks. bye.

Post-call notes (auto): shared links in chat: bench sheet (https://app.redwood/bench/nimble), config gist (https://gist.redwood/configs/nimble-batching.yaml), SOC2 packet (link to drive). Some links truncated in transcript.
